# Using voice recognition to measure trust during interactions with automated vehicles

Miaomiao Deng a, Jiaqi Chen a, Yue Wu a, Shu Ma a, Hongting Li b, Zhen Yang a,\*, Yi Shen c, \*\*

## A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords: Voice recognition Trust in automation Autonomous vehicle Machine learning

## A B S T R A C T

Trust in an automated vehicle system (AVs) can impact the experience and safety of drivers and passengers. This work investigates the effects of speech to measure drivers’ trust in the AVs. Seventy-five participants were randomly assigned to high-trust (the AVs with 100% correctness, 0 crash, and 4 system messages with visualauditory TORs) and low-trust group (the AVs with a correctness of 60%, a crash rate of 40%, 2 system messages with visual-only TORs). Voice interaction tasks were used to collect speech information during the driving process. The results revealed that our settings successfully induced trust and distrust states. The corresponding extracted speech feature data of the two trust groups were used for back-propagation neural network training and evaluated for its ability to accurately predict the trust classification. The highest classification accuracy of trust was 90.80%. This study proposes a method for accurately measuring trust in automated vehicles using voice recognition.

## 1. Introduction

Trust in automation has been the focus of substantial research in recent years with the development of artificial intelligence (e.g., Hoff and Bashir, 2015; Lee and See, 2004; Hergeth et al., 2016). The widely accepted definition of trust in automation was proposed by Lee and See (2004) as the attitude that an agent will use to help achieve a person’s goals in a situation characterized by uncertainty and vulnerability. In addition, Deutsch (1960) has defined trust as a behavioral state of vulnerability. Scholars have widely accepted that trust is a dynamic process (Lee and Moray, 1994; Wickens and Hollands, 2000; Mayer et al., 1995). An operator’s trust in a system is influenced by past experiences that are relevant to the automated system (Muir and Moray, 1996). As such, trust is a complex and multifaceted construct that is shaped by various factors and can evolve over time. Notably, trust can determine the way people interact with technology (Hoff and Bashir, 2015). If there is insufficient human trust in automation, then there may be widespread rejection of its use, which is equivalent to undermining the potential benefits of automation (Parasuraman and Riley, 1997). On the other hand, if there is excessive trust in the system, then there may be automation misuse, such as completely relying on the autopilot function and failing to monitor the vehicle and react properly (Golson, 2016). Therefore, maintaining a relatively appropriate trust level may be crucial to the safe use and operation of automated systems. The term ‘appropriate trust’ is also called calibrated trust, which refers to the correspondence between a person’s trust in automation and the automation’s capabilities, according to Lee and See (2004).

While automated vehicle technology progresses, potentially leading to a safer and more efficient traffic environment, drivers’ level of trust has been recognized as a key determinant of highly-automated driving efficiency and safety (Ekman et al., 2018). For instance, Hergeth et al. (2016) reported a negative relationship between the self-reported trust and monitoring frequency in highly-automated driving systems. Previous research consistently showed that higher reported trust was associated with a higher take-over time (TOT) and a lower minimum time-to-collision (min TTC) (Korber ¨ et al., 2018; Payre et al., 2015). Appropriate trust in driving automation is of great importance to ensure safety.

The main purpose of studying trust in the automated vehicle system (AVs) is to establish trust calibration such that the driver maintains an appropriate level of trust (GAO et al., 2021). One of the most direct ways to calibrate trust is to monitor the driver’s trust level in real time and intervene when the driver is over trusting or distrusting the system (i.e., De Visser et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2022). Ultimately, the development of timely and convenient measurements of trust will enable trust calibration in the interaction between drivers and automated vehicles.

## 1.1. Measurements of trust in automation

There are three basic approaches currently used in trust measurements: self-reporting, monitoring behavioral factors, and measuring physiological attributes associated with trust. As a well-established and traditional measure of trust, self-reports tend to have high validity and are easy to use, which are also the only direct measure of trust according to Kohn et al. (2021). However, such reports are affected by subjectivity and biases (Pop et al., 2014), and they also require task interruption and do not perfectly capture trust in real time (Azevedo-Sa et al., 2020). Behavioral measures offer a more robust way to measure trust while minimizing disruption and eliminating the bias associated with self-reporting. Kohn et al. (2021) reported the common trust behaviors include compliance, reliance, and active distrust, such as intervening with or taking over from the automation. However, the scope of application is limited and it is still difficult to capture the real-time dynamics of trust in automation. Moreover, physiological and neural measures aim to capture the results of complex cognitive processes related to trust, which has proven promising for measuring trust in real time (Kohn et al., 2021). These common physiological and neural approaches, including eye gaze tracking (Elkins and Derrick, 2013), heart rate change (Waytz et al., 2014), electrodermal activity (EDA), and electroencephalogram (EEG) (Akash et al., 2018), provide objective evidence of trust, with high resolution into the temporal aspects of trust, which enables reliable trust measurement in real time (Hopko and Mehta, 2021). However, all these methods suffer from some unique drawbacks, requiring extensive expertise and planning to apply correctly (Korber ¨ et al., 2018). Additionally, each of these measures involves complex procedures and requires specialized hardware or wearable devices, which can be uncomfortable for users and difficult to popularize, especially considering the costs of equipment development and manufacturing.

In summary, the current measurements of trust in automation have multiple limitations, and it is necessary to develop more timely, convenient, and comfortable measurement approaches.

## 1.2. Speech trust recognition

Belli and Broncano (2017) suggested that trust can be considered a meta-emotion, such that it precedes first-order emotions, which can generate a constellation of emotions from anger to love. Moreover, research has shown that emotion can be an outcome of trust, particularly when trust is violated (Conway and Briner, 2002). Trust is mainly an affective process, molded by cognitive (analytic and analogical) processes, ultimately influencing individuals’ behaviors and speaking (Lee and See, 2004). Previous research has provided evidence supporting the existence of an affective component in trust. Fahim et al. (2021) found strong correlations between positive emotions and trusting beliefs in the context of automated system usage, while negative emotions such as hostility and loneliness were negatively correlated with trust. This finding is consistent with previous studies (Jensen et al., 2020; Avetisian et al., 2022), suggesting that individuals’ emotional experiences are connected to their level of trust.

Notably, the emotive content in the speech signal provides extra information about the speaker’s psychological state (Pravena and Govind, 2017). Vocal parameters can be used to index the degrees of intensity that are typical for different emotions and differentiate valence or quality aspects (Banse and Scherer, 1996). These results have enabled the development of helpful technology, namely speech emotion recognition, which identifies and extracts different emotion-related speech features from a database, and then designs and models classifiers to recognize emotions (Swain et al., 2018). Numerous studies have reported that humans can infer emotional and mental states from vocal expression. For instance, Krajewski et al. (2008) implemented fatigue state detection based on acoustic features in human voices. Pan et al. (2018) employed voice features to establish a model for predicting depression. Prior research has demonstrated significant accuracy in emotion recognition using the speech feature of Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCC), encompassing emotions such as happiness, sadness, anger, neutral and disgust emotions (e.g., Bhimavarapu et al., 2021; Lalitha et al., 2015; Dolka et al., 2021). Thus, it is reasonable to assume that different trust states are likely associated with distinct vocal cues. Speech emotion recognition has the potential to be used in trust recognition.

Several studies have already demonstrated the association between voice attributes and trust. For example, Elkins and Derrick (2013) used voice recognition to measure trust during interactions with embodied conversational agents, which revealed that vocal pitch was inversely related to trust. Levitan and Hirschberg (2022) found that interviewers tend to speak louder, use shorter turns, and have a faster speech rate when they lacked trust in their conversational partners. Pepino et al. (2020) aimed to predict the degree of trust towards a virtual assistant by analyzing the vocal features of the user, and they indicated that in high trust conditions, most subjects spoke at a faster pace and with a higher pitch. Gauder et al. (2020) also confirmed a similar observation: users with different levels of trust exhibited variability in the syllable rate feature. Waber et al. (2015) suggest that the emphasis on words (a combination of pitch and loudness) can reflect the speaker’s trust during a new trust relationship or after a trust violation. Li et al. (2023) reveal that high levels of trust are associated with increased F1 (the formant with the lowest frequency) and F2 (the second formant) in individuals’ vocalizations. Besides, their study employed a random forest model to identify the most crucial lexical and acoustic cues of trust—context sentiment, formants, fundamental frequency, and MFCC, which showed the possibility of using conversational data to measure trust in human-AI teaming. However, there does not appear to be any work that determined whether sound can effectively be used to measure trust in vehicle automation.

On the other hand, voice interaction has become an essential part of the vehicle network and one of the significant features of AVs (Huang and Huang, 2018). With increasing levels of automation, the driver will have more time and choice to perform various tasks other than driving, and this opens new avenues for interaction, such as gestures, speech, and eye gaze (Murali et al., 2021). Voice-based interaction can potentially enhance safety, drastically reducing driver distraction and visual cognitive load by allowing drivers to keep their hands on the wheel and eyes on the road (Huang and Huang, 2018). Ultimately, the trust of drivers in the AVs may be conveniently distinguished via routine voice interaction.

## 1.3. Aim of this study

The presence of diverse noise inside and outside the vehicle poses a significant challenge to the practical implementation of speech-based trust recognition. However, advancements in speech recognition technology and its increasing integration into vehicle voice interaction systems offer promising potential for non-intrusive psychological state recognition, including trust in the AVs. Therefore, the objective of this study is to utilize speech recognition technology to assess varying levels of trust in automation within a controlled laboratory setting. The findings from this research can provide insights for the future implementation of speech recognition systems in real-world driving scenarios.

Choi and Ji (2015) proposed three dimensions for trust in vehicle automation: system transparency (the extent to which users can predict and understand the operation of vehicle automation), technical competence (the degree of user perception regarding the performance of vehicles), and situation management (the user’s belief that they can recover control in a situation whenever desired). Thus, this work used different components (i.e., system transparency, technical competence, and situation management) of trust in vehicle automation to elicit two distinct trust level conditions.

While participating under these two trust level conditions, drivers were asked to complete voice interaction tasks. The speech in the corresponding states was collected, which was used for feature extraction, feature selection, classification and prediction model training, model validation and explaining. We mainly used a back-propagation neural network (BP-NN) to distinguish diverse levels of trust, with the extracted speech data as input and the self-reported trust labels and scores as the output, thus verifying the feasibility and predictability of voice as a measurement of trust in the AVs.

## 2. Method

In this study, the capability of the automation was set to level 3 (L3) based on the Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE; SAE International, 2014) criteria. L3 automated driving can provide complete automation when automated driving features are engaged, allowing drivers to perform secondary tasks. Drivers only need to monitor the environment when receiving a take-over request (TOR; Gold et al., 2013). Therefore, setting the automation L3 is appropriate in designing an experiment to investigate trust during automated driving (Yoo et al., 2022).

## 2.1. Participants

Seventy-five participants with valid Chinese driving licenses were recruited. The participants in the high-trust group had an average driving license holding period of 2.78 years (SD = 1.92) and were within the age range of 19–27 years (19 female; 17 male; M = 22.69 years; SD = 2.07 years). On the other hand, the participants in the low-trust group had an average driving license holding period of 2.18 years (SD = 1.89) and were within the age range of 19–26 years (22 female; 17 male; M = 22.15 years; SD = 1.56 years). None of the participants had experience with adaptive cruise control or AVs. Informed consent was obtained from each participant, following the research protocol approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Department of Psychology at Zhejiang Sci-Tech University.

## 2.2. Apparatus

This study uses a driving simulation platform consisting of driving simulator software (STISIM DRIVE M100K, Systems Technology Inc., Hawthorne, CA, USA) and an operating system (Logitech MOMO, Newark, CA, USA). Specifically, it includes a force-feedback steering wheel, pedal units (including brake, gas pedal, and clutch pedals), an adjustable driver’s seat, two computers, an INTECH IWB 72-inch LED screen with 1920 × 1080 pixel resolution, and a sound system consisting of four speech controllers and a recorder (Samsung YV 150X). The driving simulation platform is shown in Fig. 1.

## 2.3. Measurements and materials

The checklist of trust between people and automation (CTPA) questionnaire (Jian et al., 2000) was used to measure participants subjective trust. The questionnaire contains 12 items involving both trust and distrust dimensions. All questionnaires are measured on a 7-point Likert scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

To make the speech collection more natural, we selected the speech interaction tasks that are commonly used during driving according to Simmons et al. (2017). The speech evaluation task materials are listed in Table 1.

## 2.4. Experimental design

In a driving simulator experiment, participants operate a self-driving vehicle (SAE level 3) on a highway. The study is conducted under a dualtask paradigm, where participants are asked to drive safely as the primary task. As a secondary task, they need to play a game on a tablet PC to reduce the impact of boredom, which mimics a natural scenario.

This study adopts a 2 × 2 mixed design to induce different levels of trust and collect the speech in the corresponding states. The betweensubject independent variable consists of two trust levels: high-trust and low-trust. The within-subject independent variable is the test time, specifically before and after driving with the L3 AVs. The dependent variables are the participants’ trust levels for the AVs and the corresponding speech features.

Notably, a study by Chavaillaz et al. (2016) showed that reduced system reliability resulted in lower levels of trust toward automation, which managed the trust level by manipulating different competence conditions (low reliability: 60%, medium reliability: 80%, and high reliability: 100%). According to Niu et al. (2018), providing information to users that allows them to perceive and understand the autonomous vehicle’s state increases their trust in the AVs. Compared to visual-only feedback, prior research has shown that integrating visual and auditory channels provides participants with additional insights into driving scenes, enhancing their understanding of the driving system and increasing trust levels (Basantis et al., 2021). Herein, system technical competence and transparency were manipulated to create two trust levels (high-trust and low-trust).

To obtain two distinct levels of trust, we manipulated different experimental conditions based on Chavaillaz et al. (2016) and Niu et al. (2018). These conditions corresponded to the trust dimensions proposed by Choi and Ji (2015), as outlined in Table 2. For the high-trust group, the AVs was set to be completely correct to establish a high level of competency. Correct actions mean the system accurately predict and safely handle incidents. As a result, the driver did not need to take over at all during the formal experiment. However, to ensure consistency in the experiment, takeover exercises were still conducted during the practice course, with the high-trust group receiving both auditory and visual TORs. Moreover, the system crash rate was set to 0% to develop high dependability, and no system malfunctions occurred. The human-machine interface (HMI) displayed four current system status messages, such as the vehicle speed, driving mode (manual/automatic), vehicle status with navigation route, and current operation (lane change, braking, acceleration, deceleration). The vehicle ‘health’ icon provided messages about the system’s current working order, such as the state of the tires, brakes, network, and battery level (Stephenson et al., 2020). Fig. 2 shows the information employed in the HMI screen for the two experimental conditions.

In contrast, for the low-trust group, the AVs was correct in 60% of the trials, demonstrating low competence. Incorrect actions mean the system accurately predict but cannot handle incidents, so the driver needed to randomly take over twice during five trials, and involved only visual TORs. The system crash rate of the low-trust group is 40%, demonstrating low dependability, so the system will break down twice during simulated driving. The first system crash involved a less dangerous consequence: hitting the crash barrier and stopping the operation of the driving system. The second system crash was more serious, hitting a stopping vehicle and ending the experiment. The HMI screen displayed only messages related to the vehicle speed and driving mode (manual/ automatic), excluding the ‘health’ icon and vehicle status information. Additionally, while the actual level of trust can only be ascertained through experimental manipulation, we have categorized the groups as high-trust and low-trust based on similar grouping names from previous research (e.g. Zhang et al., 2021).

## 2.5. Procedure

The entire procedure is illustrated in Fig. 3. The participants read, signed an informed consent form, and completed a demographic survey questionnaire. Then the experimenter introduced the L3 AVs to the participants. Participants filled out CTPA questionnaires to measure initial trust level. Next, they need to be familiar with the speech task materials in advance, as shown in Table 1. The navigation task’s contents and the evaluation task’s structure remained fixed. Participants were required to select the corresponding words and scores based on their expectations of the system (before driving) or the system’s current performance (after driving). Then they were instructed to speak the relevant materials in a naturally relaxed state, while a recorder collected their voices. Subsequently, the participants were then randomly assigned to the high-trust or low-trust groups and completed the corresponding practice course. The practice course consisted of three sections. The first section was a 5 km manual driving exercise. The second section was a 5 km takeover exercise, in which they explained the meaning of the system status messages and TORs for different groups. In the high-trust group, if there was a need to take over, the system would send out the voice signal ‘please take over’ with a 7 s lead time, and the driving mode in the HMI screen would change from automated mode to manual mode. In the low-trust group, there was no voice signal to take over, only the change of driving mode on the HMI screen. Afterward, participants were introduced to a Tetris game (Electronic Arts, 2013) on a tablet computer as a secondary task. This choice was made because playing games requires continuous attention and can be considered one of the most common non-driving activities observed in real-world autonomous driving scenarios (Sivak and Schoettle, 2015). Participants were told that safe driving (accident-free driving in compliance with traffic rules) was the primary goal and were allowed to participate in the secondary task only when driving automatically, while being responsible for supervising the system (Kraus et al., 2019). Therefore, in case of an accident or traffic violation, the participant fee shall be deducted as a fine. In addition, they should try to achieve a high score in the Tetris game to obtain an additional prize. In the third section, participants completed the practice of taking over and secondary tasks.

In the formal experimental scenario, participants need to complete a total driving length of 18 km, where five random critical events will occur. These events include one instance of motorcycle overtaking, two instances of obstruction ahead, and two instances of emergency braking by the vehicle ahead. Each participant took about 20 min to complete the whole experimental driving route.

After the formal driving trial, participants were again asked to perform a navigation task and a system evaluation task, followed by filling out a CTPA questionnaire to measure posttask trust level. At the end of the experiment, participants were given a financial reward, and they were verbally asked about the problems and psychological conditions they encountered during the driving simulation. The entire experiment lasted approximately 40 min.

## 2.6. Data analysis

## 2.6.1. Questionnaire data

All participants completed the CTPA questionnaires at the beginning and the end of the experiment, which yielded 150 valid CTPA questionnaire data, with 78 for the high-trust group and 72 for the low-trust group. For the data analysis, a mixed two-factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted to check the effectiveness of the trust level manipulation. All statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 23 (IBM Corp, Armonk, NY, United States). Assumptions of sphericity were assessed using Mauchly’s test, and if violated, Greenhouse-Geisser estimates were used in the repeated measures calculations. The statistical threshold for significance was set to 0.05 (two-tailed). Partial eta squared $( \eta _ { p } ^ { 2 } )$ was used as the effect size for ANOVA results (Cohen, 1988). Post hoc analyzes were run with Bonferroni correction.

## 2.6.2. Speech data

First, the speech materials were grouped with scores in the CTPA questionnaire for speech processing. The CTPA questionnaire provides separate values for trust (items 1–5) and distrust dimensions (items 6–12). We reversed the distrust score and averaged it with the trust score to obtain the final trust score. The present study employed a median split to divide the subjects into high and low-trust groups based on their trust scores (Median = 3.91). Iacobucci et al. (2015) demonstrated that employing the median as a threshold for a continuous variable presents a more reliable approach in discerning individuals with high or low levels of a specific attribute. For pre-driving speech, forty participants’ speech samples were defined as high-trust speech, and thirty-five participants’ speech samples were defined as low-trust speech. For post-driving speech, the post-driving speech samples of 36 participants were labeled as high-trust, and 39 were labeled as low-trust. Then, the results were processed to generate the speech files using Audacity (verison.3.1.3). We excluded different words freely chosen by the participants in the evaluation task or pauses in all speech materials to ensure consistency in the context of speech data. The speech material was extracted from five equally valid evaluation texts and one navigation speech text. Eight speech files failed to be collected for device reasons, and 892 valid speech files were finally obtained.

## 2.6.3. Feature extraction and reduction

In this study, we extracted the trust-related acoustic features of each speech file mentioned in the introduction. In total, we extracted 24 features, as shown in Table 3.

These features are commonly studied in general speech research as well. To ensure consistency in the magnitude of input data, the data were normalized to [− 1,1] and stored together with their classification labels. In addition, gender-based normalization was performed on all the acoustic features to account for the potential influence of gender. All feature extraction was implemented using Python’s Librosa package (McFee et al., 2015).

| (2)Speech rate | Speech rate is estimated by calculating the ratio of voiced frames to total frames. |
| (3-4)Mean, SD(f0) | Mean and Standard deviation of fundamental frequency (f0). The fundamental frequency corresponds to the physiological parameter of the vibration frequency of the vocal folds measured in hertz (Hz) (Hirst and De Looze, 2021). |

## 2.7. Machine learning algorithms

Considering that this work has a clear set of target variables (i.e., trust in the AVs) and corresponding attributes (i.e., acoustic features), we employed a supervised machine learning (ML) approach (Russel and Norvig, 2010). Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are highly parameterized and nonlinear models, which makes them particularly suitable for ill-defined and highly nonlinear problems involving multiple variables (Graupe, 2013). This study utilized the Back Propagation Neural Network (Rumelhart et al., 1986) as the primary method for trust classification and prediction. This modified and optimized version of the ANN has gained popularity among researchers in the field of ANNs, particularly for classification problems (Cui et al., 2021). The machine learning analysis used in this study consisted of four phases: feature selection, model training, classification and prediction evaluation, and model explanation, as shown in Fig. 4. We computed the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for each feature and retained speech features with VIF scores below 10, following the recommendation of O’Brien (2007), as a VIF value exceeding 10 indicates significant or severe multi-collinearity. The classification process was defined as follows: the trained BP neural network was used to classify the categories to which the test data belonged, and the accuracy rate of each class was calculated based on the classification results. The acoustic features were randomly divided into training and testing sets with a ratio of 7:3, and ten-fold cross-validation was employed (Zhang, 2000). Grouped k-fold cross-validation considers the grouping structure of the data. It ensures that samples from the same participant are always kept together in the same fold, eliminating the possibility of cross-subject recognition due to participant-specific acoustic properties and reducing overly optimistic estimates of model performance (Li et al., 2023). The training parameters are considered to achieve the best neural network architecture based on training datasets (See Table 4).

The evaluation indicators of the effectiveness of the classification model also include the Precision, Recall, Accuracy, and F-measure. Higher scores on these indicators indicate that the model performs more accurately. The evaluation metrics are defined as follows:

$$
\text {Precision} = \frac {\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{FP}}\tag{1}
$$

$$
\text {Recall} = \frac {\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{FN}}\tag{2}
$$

The parameters of the BP -NN model.

| Parameters |  |
| --- | --- |
| Number of layers Neurons | 4Input:16 |
|  | First hidden layer:128 Second hidden layer:64 |
| Activation function | Output:2 Relu Function |
| Optimizer | Adam Gradient Descent |
| Learning rate | 0.001 |
| Dropout probability | 0.5 (Srivastava et al., 2014). |

$$
\text {Accuracy} = \frac {\mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{TN}}{\mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{FP} + \mathrm{TN} + \mathrm{FN}}\tag{3}
$$

$$
\text {F - measure} = \frac {(\beta^ {2} + 1) \times \text {Precision} \times \text {Recall}}{\beta^ {2} \times \text {Precision} + \text {Recall}}\tag{4}
$$

True positive (TP) is the number of samples categorized correctly in class trust, and false positive (FP) refers to the number of samples misclassified in the trusted class. False negative (FN) is the number of samples belonging to the trusted class that are misclassified in the distrust class, and true negative (TN) is the number of samples not in the trusted class that are classified in the distrust class. The F-measure is evenly balanced when β = 1 (Sokolova et al., 2006).

After obtaining the speech classifications, the same features were used to train the prediction model. The training parameters and speech samples of the prediction model were identical to those employed in training the BP-NN classification model. Subsequently, the predicted trust values were compared against the ground truth, representing the corresponding trust scores derived from the CTPA questionnaire under identical labels. To enhance the overall reliability of our predictions, we employed a normalization technique to calibrate the model’s output trust scores within the range of 0–1, thereby mitigating the impact of significant fluctuations in actual scores. The adjusted R-squared $( \mathbf { R } _ { \mathsf { a d j } } ^ { 2 } )$ was a modified version of R-squared that considers the number of independent variables in a regression model, indicating how well the data points fit the curve on a scale from 0 to 1. The Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) represents the standard deviation of the prediction errors. It serves as a measure for assessing the concentration of actual data points around the best-fit line. A higher $\mathbf { R } _ { \mathrm { a d j } } ^ { 2 }$ -value approaching one and a smaller RMSE indicate the better performance of the model. RMSE and $\mathbf { R } _ { \mathrm { a d j } } ^ { 2 }$ can be calculated as follows (Rustam et al., 2020):

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 4. Machine learning analysis processing flow.

$$
\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt {\frac {1}{\mathrm{n}} \sum_ {\mathrm{i} = 1} ^ {\mathrm{n}} \left(\mathrm{y} _ {\mathrm{i}} - \hat {\mathrm{y}} _ {\mathrm{i}}\right) ^ {2}}\tag{5}
$$

$$
R _ {\mathrm{adj}} ^ {2} = 1 - \frac {\sum_ {\mathrm{i} = 1} ^ {\mathrm{n}} \left(\mathrm{y} _ {\mathrm{i}} - \hat {\mathrm{y}} _ {\mathrm{i}}\right) ^ {2} (\mathrm{n} - \mathrm{k} - 1)}{\sum_ {\mathrm{i} = 1} ^ {\mathrm{n}} \left(\mathrm{y} _ {\mathrm{i}} - \overline {{\mathrm{y}}} _ {\mathrm{i}}\right) ^ {2} (\mathrm{n} - 1)}\tag{6}
$$

where $\mathrm { y _ { i } }$ represents the true value that was collected by the CTPA questionnaire, $\hat { \mathbf { y } } _ { \mathrm { i } }$ indicates the predicted value, $\overline { { \mathrm { y _ { i } } } }$ indicates the average number of true values, and n represents the number of samples, while k denotes the number of input parameters in the prediction model.

In this study, we employed two widely used machine-learning interpretability methods to explain the performance of our topperforming model, namely Variable Importance Plot (VIP) and Partial Dependence Plot (PDP). Notably, recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of PDP in revealing causal inferences between input features and the response variable (Zhao and Hastie, 2021). Li et al. (2023) also effectively demonstrated a non-linear shift in trust by observing changes in conversational features through the application of the aforementioned explanation methods, providing valuable insights into the explanation pipeline of this research. In particular, the significance of each variable in predicting the response variable is quantified through variable importance plots. The Partial Dependence Plot (PDP) depicts the relationship between the response variable and a set of input features while considering the influence of other variables through marginalization (Friedman, 2001).

In addition, four additional ML approaches were employed to determine whether the proposed model’s advantage was significant. These approaches were commonly used supervised machine learning algorithms: Random Forest (RF), K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) (Uddin et al., 2019).

## 3.1. Trust questionnaire

The descriptive statistics of CTPA questionnaires are displayed in Table 5. A 2 (trust group: high-trust and low-trust) × 2 (test time: pre-driving and post-driving) repeated measures ANOVA was performed for trust scores. There was a significant effect of the group $\left[ F \left( 1 ,   7 3 \right) = \right.$ 75.43, $p < 0.001, \eta_{p}^{2} = 0.508]$ and the test time $F(1,73)=8.506,p=$ 0.005, $\eta _ { p } ^ { 2 }   =   0 . 1 0 4 ]$ on the trust scores. Moreover, the interaction between the group and test time was significant $F\left(1,73\right)=93.32,p<$ $0.001,\ \eta_{p}^{2}   =   0.561]$ . A simple effect test with pairwise comparisons revealed that after driving with the $\mathbf { A } \mathbf { V } \mathbf { s } ,$ trust in the high-trust group (M $4.92, SD = 0.86$ was significantly higher in the low-trust group $( M =$ $2 . 5 0 ,   S D = 0 . 9 2 )$ . At the same time, the two groups had no significant difference in trust before driving. As illustrated in ${ \operatorname { F i g . } } 5 ,$ trust in the high-trust group increased from pre-driving to post-driving, and trust in the low-trust group decreased from pre-driving to post-driving.

## 3.2. Trust recognition with speech

## 3.2.1. Trust classification model

A total of 24 acoustic features were initially extracted, and two features (pitch\_min, pitch\_median) with a value of 0 calculated by the Librosa package were excluded. Moreover, subsequent identification of multicollinearity issues resulted in removing six features (pitch $\mathsf { s d } ,$ pitch\_mean, F4\_mean, intensity\_min, intensity\_max, F3\_sd) with a VIF>10. As a result, only 16 features were retained for further analysis, as indicated in Fig. 6.

Fig. 7 shows the performance results of the five classification models in a matrix form. Accordingly, each row of the matrix represents the actual attribution category of the sample, and each column represents the prediction category, showing the results of four evaluation metrics for five machine learning classifiers, as shown in Table 6. The results indicate that the BP-NN and RF models achieved classification accuracies of over 80%, while the average accuracy of the other classifiers was approximately 60%. Notably, the BP-NN classification model outperformed the other models with an exceptional accuracy rate of 90.8%, followed by RF (85.10%), KNN (74.30%), LDA (64.20%), and SVM (61.70%). This preliminary result suggests that different trust states can cause vocal separation. Moreover, the BP-NN method demonstrates superior accuracy in trust classification compared to other ML approaches in this study.

## 3.2.2. Trust prediction model

The Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) technique primarily serves as a classification method and is commonly employed for dimensionality reduction and feature extraction. Consequently, this approach was not employed for prediction training. The outcome indicators of each pre-diction model are presented in Table 7. The results of both metrics indicate that, with the exception of the SVM and KNN models, the remaining two demonstrate $\mathbf { R } _ { \mathrm { a d j } } ^ { 2 }$ -values exceeding 0.50, accompanied by an RMSE of approximately 0.1. Notably, the BP-NN model outperforms other models, exhibiting the lowest RMSE(0.102) and the highest $\mathbf { R } _ { \mathrm { a d j } } ^ { 2 }$ (0.668), which means the model can explain the 66.8% variance of trust in the AVs.

## 3.2.3. Model explanation

Considering the superior performance of BP-NN algorithms in classification tasks compared to alternative approaches, we have opted to employ VIP and PDP techniques for investigating the relationships between features and trust. The importance of the features in the classification model is illustrated in Fig. 8. The most important feature is standardized to 100%, while the relative importance of other features is adjusted proportionally.

## 4. Discussion

A BP-NN model was developed to accurately classify and predict the level of a driver’s trust in automated vehicles based on speech data. We divided the participants into two groups (high-trust and low-trust) by manipulating system technical competence and system transparency, and we observed distinct trust separation between these two groups. The BP-NN models developed in this study showed high classification accuracies about 90.8%, and the prediction model showed a satisfactory fitting effect $( \mathsf{R}_{ adj }^2 = 0.668 )$ . In current trust measures, accurately capturing the real-time dynamics of trust in automation has proven challenging using self-reports and behavioral measures alone. While physiological and neural measures show promise in enabling real-time trust measurement, their full implementation in the real world is limited by the need for specialized hardware, complex procedures, and expertise (Kohn et al., 2021). Therefore, we investigated a portable and non-invasive real-time trust measurement method. Due to the high degree of naturalness and functionality, voice interaction has been widely used in the car. Furthermore, a robust ML algorithm in combination with emotion recognition allows for speech to be exploited as a measurement of trust.

Our findings demonstrate significant effects of intensity, MFCC variation, and fundamental frequency variation on trust classification. Intensity is a prosodic feature that represents the relative loudness or volume of a sound. Our results align with the prior study that showed that higher-intensity speech was associated with lower trust levels (Levitan and Hirschberg, 2022). This study represents the first empirical evidence demonstrating the efficacy of intensity in classifying individuals’ trust in the AVs.

Moreover, spectral features are commonly employed to represent the physical characteristics of vocal organs. MFCC, as a widely used spectral feature, can effectively simulate the human auditory perception system, thereby improving the performance of speech emotion recognition (Ahmad et al., 2015). Nwe et al. (2003) found that the spectral energy features differ for emotions of different valence and arousal levels. Therefore, trust, as an emotional process, can also be discriminated using spectral features. To our surprise, our study emphasizes the significance of MFCC\_sd as a crucial feature in trust classification, exhibiting a positive correlation with the likelihood of being categorized as high-trust. This finding provides fresh insights into speech-based trust recognition.

Our findings highlight the significance of f0 variance in trust classification. However, contrary to prior research by Li et al. (2023), our study revealed that a higher f0 variance within a specific range corresponds to a greater probability of being categorized as low-trust speech. This discrepancy may be attributed to variations in speech tasks and usage scenarios. Levitan and Hirschberg (2022) have emphasized that speech characteristics can significantly vary based on speakers’ cultural and linguistic backgrounds, whether the conversation partner is human or machine, and the specific speech task. Our study focused on a fixed voice task that simulates individual interactions with an in-car voice assistant, where drivers need to naturally read materials in order to issue instructions. In contrast, most studies involve more spontaneous human-human dialogues. Fuchs et al. (2015) have pointed out that spontaneous speech is less prepared, making speakers unable to plan the prosodic structure thoroughly. Furthermore, their study demonstrated that f0 declination varies based on the speech task, with more significant variability observed in f0 declination for read speech than spontaneous speech data. Hence, more studies should further investigate the impact of speech tasks and the communication context on trust classification and explore the underlying mechanisms involved.

In principle, the high accuracy of the classification model should correspond to more pronounced trends in the PDPs. In this study, the observed relatively flat trends in the PDPs can be explained in several ways. On one hand, the trust score distribution encompassed a total of 150 data points, with a small standard deviation $(M = 3.85, SD = 1.20)$ $Min=1.00,\;Max=6.00$ . This minimal variance in trust scores could potentially lead to limited variation being reflected in the PDPs. Alternatively, the explanation could be attributed to multi-layered structure and fully-connected layers of neural networks. Model performance tends to stabilize following multiple iterations of training, at which point the sensitivity of the nodes to the numerical values of features decreases, and the impact of individual features on node activation diminishes (Grégoire et al., 2017). According to LeCun et al. (2015), employing multiple non-linear layers, usually with a depth of 5–20, enables a neural network to execute intricate functions on its inputs, which implies that the combination of multiple input variables can have a more complex effect on the activation of a node. Consequently, the nature of the algorithm may lead to individual features alone not being influential enough to classify or predict trust, even if they are highly ranked in VIP. However, the model demonstrate improved performance when multiple features are combined.

We believe that our study is the first to use voice recognition to measure trust in automated driving scenarios, and this study may lay the foundation for convenient and contactless trust measurements. The proposed methodology yields a practical implication for the calibration of trust in the AVs, which can be applied to developing systems that can monitor and adjust trust levels in real time. Alternatively, it can be used for multimodal measures of trust to provide the most powerful detection, such as combining subjective, physiological, neural, and voice measures, to achieve a higher precision measurement and provide objective, systematic, and efficient standards for trust regulation systems. Based on this, the driver’s voice can be collected and analyzed in real time, during interaction with an in-car voice assistant, its trust level can be predicted, and corresponding adjustments can be provided. For instance, if there is misalignment between a person’s trust in the AVs and the AVs capabilities, it can be adjusted by presenting different system transparency messages so that drivers can perceive the vehicle’s performance more positively (Dikmen and Burns, 2017) or by employing politeness strategies (i.e., asking help, giving a reason, expressing gratitude (Lee and Lee, 2022) to restore the calibrated trust level.

Considering this work’s experimental and preliminary nature, future research should address certain limitations. First, although the BP-NN method used in this study is suitable for classification and demonstrates satisfactory fitting results, it is essential to acknowledge the strengths and weaknesses of this approach. Artificial neural networks (ANNs) can approximate any continuous function. However, their complex and hyper-parameterized structure often makes it challenging to interpret the underlying relationships and relative importance of predictors or covariates in the model. To address this issue, we employed machine-learning interpretability methods to explain the performance of our prediction model (see Supplementary Material for more details). However, it is worth noting that the interpretability effect was not exceptionally high in this study. The main reason for this issue is the limited dataset (892) used in this work, which challenges the model in adaptively discovering patterns. Additionally, the complexity of neural network models further complicates the understanding and interpreting of their associated predictors. Therefore, it is advisable to employ transparency-based ML models and additional post hoc interpretation methods on larger datasets to better understand the relationship between trust levels and speech features. Second, the level of trust induced in the laboratory is limited compared to real driving because driving simulators do not incorporate physical risk, and the consequences of the user’s actions are low or imaginary (De Winter et al., 2012). Additionally, it is notable that speech collection in the laboratory involves meticulous control over environmental conditions, while real-world driving environments often involve background noise and distortion. To address these limitations, we suggest that future studies include real-world validation on real roads with a natural set of incidents and incorporate de-noising techniques. These will help ensure the findings’ validity and generalizability in real-world driving scenarios. Third, the number of youth and new driver respondents was relatively higher than other respondents. Previous research has pointed out that individuals ages, experiences, and personality traits can relate to trust in automation (Molnar et al., 2018). Accordingly, a larger sample with varying age levels, driver experience, and personality traits should be recruited to improve the model’s prediction accuracy and generalize the implications. In addition, although the two distinct levels of overall trust in the AVs were successfully induced by specific tasks where we extracted the exact words for each driver, there are more voice interactions and more unrestricted situations that arise in natural driving environments. In short, future work should focus on collecting various task-oriented dialogues with the naturalness of interactions and identifying different trust categories using speech combined with additional phonetic features such as text characteristics to realize a genuinely portable measurement of trust. Finally, investigations with multimodal measures as model output variables and combining other unobtrusive measures (e.g., facial expression and behavior indicators) as input variables may improve the measurement reliability.

## 5. Conclusion

Trust is essential for safe autonomous driving. However, conveniently measuring trust in real time presents a challenge. The current study investigated voice recognition as a measurement of trust in autonomous driving. To accomplish this, a driving simulator experiment was designed to induce a high and low level of trust by manipulating the system’s technical competence and system transparency. Two levels of trust were successfully generated, and the speech in the corresponding states was collected. We found that the BP-NN algorithm was adopted as the primary tool for classifying and predicting the trust in the AVs yielded the best performance with a classification rate of 90.8% and a best fit value $( \mathbf { R } _ { \mathsf { a d j } } ^ { 2 } )$ of 0.668. Thus, trust states can be separated and predicted in the acoustic domain with reasonable accuracy, demonstrating that voice recognition is a viable option for measuring trust in the AVs.

This work makes the first step toward exploring voice recognition as a measurement of trust in the AVs and provides a basis for contactless trust measurements. Moreover, it can offer insight into trust calibration in the interaction between drivers and automated vehicles and enhance drivers’ understanding of autonomous driving.
